q: Headlights must be on from…
a: ½ hour before sunset to ½ hour after sunrise
w: 1 hour before sunset to 1 hour after sunrise
e: Also any time poor light means you can't clearly see people or vehicles 150 m away.
s: headlights are required to be turned on between one-half hour before sunset and one-half hour after sunrise

q: Using high beams, you must switch to low beams when an oncoming vehicle is within…
a: 150 metres
e: 150 m for oncoming. 60 m when following.
s: When you use high-beam headlights, remember to switch to low beams within 150 metres of an oncoming vehicle.

q: You must use low beams when you're following another vehicle within…
a: 60 metres
e: Following = 60 m (the smaller number). Oncoming = 150 m.
s: Use your low beams when you are less than 60 metres behind another vehicle unless you are passing it.

q: By law, you must report a collision to police if someone is injured, or if damage to vehicles or property is more than…
e: The current handbook says $5,000. Older books may show a lower amount.
s: By law, you must report any collision to the police when there are injuries or damage to vehicles or other property exceeding $5,000.

q: You're driving in fog. Which lights should you use?
a: Low beams (plus fog lights if you have them)
e: High beams reflect off the fog and make it harder to see.
s: Use your low-beam headlights. High beams reflect off the moisture droplets in the fog, making it harder to see.

q: Do anti-lock brakes (ABS) shorten your stopping distance?
a: Not necessarily: they stop the wheels locking so you can still steer
e: Don't expect to stop sooner just because you have ABS.
s: Although anti-lock braking systems help to prevent wheel lock, you should not expect the stopping distance for your vehicle to be shortened.

q: Which statement about daytime running lights is TRUE?
a: They're only for good light; in poor light, turn on your headlights
w: They light up your tail lights too
e: Daytime running lights may not turn on your tail lights, and they aren't proper headlights.
s: Your daytime running lights are not to be used as headlights during poor lighting conditions.

q: A minor collision: no one is hurt and the damage is under $5,000. What must you still do?
a: Exchange information with the other driver
e: You don't have to report it to police, but you must exchange information.
s: If damage is less than $5,000, you are still required by law to exchange information with anyone whose vehicle has been damaged.

q: When it's cold, which parts of the road freeze FIRST?
a: Shaded areas, bridges and overpasses
e: Look ahead and be ready for ice on bridges and in shade.
s: Sections of road in shaded areas or on bridges and overpasses freeze first.

q: Your car starts to skid on an icy road. What should you do?
a: Ease off the gas or brake and steer in the direction you want to go
w: Steer the opposite way from where you want to go
e: Don't oversteer. On very slippery surfaces, shift to neutral if you can.
s: Ease off on the accelerator or brake and on a very slippery surface slip the transmission into neutral if you can. Continue to steer in the direction you wish to go.

q: You need to stop fast in a car with anti-lock brakes (ABS). What should you do?
a: Press the brake pedal hard and let the ABS work, even if the pedal pulses
e: Don't let up when you feel the pulsing.
s: Press the brake pedal hard and allow the system to control wheel lock-up.

q: Your brakes suddenly fail. What should you try FIRST?
a: Pump the brake pedal
w: Pull the parking brake as hard as you can
e: Pumping may restore brake pressure. If not, apply the parking brake gently but firmly, holding the release button.
s: Try pumping the brake pedal to temporarily restore hydraulic brake pressure.

q: Your gas pedal sticks. What should you try first?
a: Lift the pedal by slipping your foot under it
w: Reach down and pull it up with your hand
Turn the engine off right away
e: Never reach down with your hands while moving. If that doesn't work: hazard lights, neutral, stop off the road.
s: First try to lift the pedal by slipping your foot under it. Do not reach down with your hands while the vehicle is moving.

q: Your right wheels drop off the pavement onto the shoulder. What should you do?
a: Grip the wheel, ease off the gas, avoid heavy braking, and steer back when under control
w: Brake hard and steer back quickly
Speed up and swerve back onto the road
e: Don't panic. Slow down first, then steer back gently.
s: Don't panic. Grip the steering wheel firmly. Take your foot off the gas pedal to slow down. Avoid heavy braking.

q: A tire blows out while you're driving. What should you do?
a: Take your foot off the gas, steer firmly where you want to go, and stop off the road
e: A blowout can shake the wheel a lot. Stay calm and steer.
s: Take your foot off the gas pedal to slow down and steer the vehicle firmly in the direction you want to go.

q: The fog gets so thick you can't keep driving. What should you do?
a: Pull completely off the road, turn on your emergency flashers, and keep your low beams on
w: Stop in your lane with flashers on
Speed up to get out of it
e: Never stop on the travelled part of the road. You could be the first link in a chain-reaction crash.
s: If the fog is too dense to continue, pull completely off the road and try to position your vehicle in a safe parking area.

q: Bright headlights from an oncoming car are blinding you at night. Where should you look?
a: Up, beyond and slightly to the right of the oncoming lights
e: Keep your eyes off the glare but on your lane.
s: When meeting oncoming vehicles with bright headlights at night, look up and beyond and slightly to the right of the oncoming lights.

q: You're in a minor collision. No one is hurt and both cars can be driven. What should you do?
a: Move the cars as far off the road as possible ("Steer it, clear it")
w: Leave the cars exactly where they are until police arrive
Block the lane with your hazard lights on
e: Moving them is especially important on busy or high-speed roads.
s: So in a minor collision with no injuries, if you can “Steer it, Clear it”.

q: To get your vehicle out of a skid, you should first:
a: Steer in the direction you want to go.
w: Steer in the opposite direction of the skid.
e: Official MTO sample question.
s: Continue to steer in the direction you wish to go.

q: It is more dangerous to drive at the maximum speed limit at night than during daytime as:
a: You cannot see as far ahead at night.
w: Your reaction time is slower at night.
Some drivers unlawfully drive with parking lights only.
The roadways are more apt to be slippery at night.
e: Official MTO sample question. Slow down at night so you don't overdrive your headlights.
s: At night and in weather conditions such as rain, snow or fog, you cannot see as far ahead, even with headlights.

q: What must every driver involved in a collision do?
a: Stay at the scene (or return to it right away) and give all possible help
w: Leave if they think it wasn't their fault
Leave once they've called their insurance
Stay only if police are already there
e: Leaving the scene of a collision is 7 demerit points and a Criminal Code offence.
s: Every driver involved in a collision must stay at the scene or return to it immediately and give all possible assistance.

q: Your headlights go out while driving at night. What should you do?
a: Check the switch; if they stay out, turn on your hazard lights and stop safely off the road
w: Keep driving with your parking lights
Drive with your high beams flashing
e: It's dangerous and illegal to drive at night without lights.
s: It is dangerous and illegal to drive at night without lights.

q: Snow removal vehicles use what kind of flashing lights?
a: Blue, visible from 150 metres
e: Never pass between plows working side by side, and never pass a moving snow plow.
s: Snow-removal vehicles on public roadways are equipped with flashing blue lights that can be seen from 150 metres.
